name: Social cryptomnesia
statement: People approve a value such as gender equality more than they approve the minority that campaigned for it, and that gap is what social cryptomnesia names.
meaning: The claim is about societies, not about one person's memory. It runs in two steps. A minority argues for a position, meets resistance, and is disliked for arguing. Later the position becomes ordinary and the group that argued for it stays disliked. Mugny and Pérez treat the second step as the price of the first: for minority influence to surface at all, they write, those who began the argument have to be forgotten. What the experiments measure is narrower than that story. A respondent rates agreement with a principle, or agreement with the group that promoted it, or agreement with the principle when the group is named alongside it. The three ratings differ, and the difference between them is the effect. No participant in any study located here was asked who won women the vote, or when, or from whom. The name says forgetting and the instrument reads approval.

origin.who: Gabriel Mugny and Juan A. Pérez
origin.note: A three-page piece in the bulletin's dossier on psychology and politics, opening on the history of French feminism and closing on an experiment with 926 Spanish respondents. Mugny and Pérez name the effect there and credit the observation to Moscovici, Lage and Naffrechoux's 1969 colour-perception study, which is the only earlier work their reference list carries alongside two of their own books. Pérez's own bibliography gives the page range as 3 to 5 and Vernet, Vala and Butera give it as 3 to 6.

evidence: The 1989 note pairs five principles with the groups that historically argued for them: liberty with anarchists, equality of the sexes with feminists, equality of races with anti-racists, respect for the environment with ecologists, and peace with pacifists. Respondents were 926 Spanish participants, most of them aged 15 to 19, split between three conditions. In the principles condition 306 people rated agreement with the principle alone, on an eight-point scale where 8 meant agreement. In the minorities condition 313 rated the groups alone. In the minority principles condition 307 rated the principle with its group attached, in the form 'feminists are right because they fight for equality between the sexes'. Approval ran highest for the principles at 7.20, lowest for the groups at 5.50, and in between at 6.14 when the two were joined, with all differences significant at a threshold of at least p < .001. Splitting respondents by their own left or right self-placement, 444 and 402 of them, left the principles untouched: 7.22 on the left against 7.19 on the right. Naming the group opened a difference of 6.25 against 6.03, reported at p < .15, and rating the groups alone gave 5.70 against 5.33 at p < .01. No effect sizes, standard deviations or test statistics accompany those means. Vernet, Vala, Amâncio and Butera took the design to feminism in 2009 with 93 participants, showing them their own higher rating of women's rights than of feminists and blaming them for it in a more or less threatening way. Their abstract reports that this produced a warmer attitude to feminists and lower hostile sexism when the threat was lower. Vernet, Vala and Butera repeated the measurement twice in 2011. In their first experiment 67 women at a large French university, mean age 20.4, rated women's rights at 12.81 and feminist movements at 6.89 on four-item 13-point scales. The rating of feminists sat on the midpoint of the scale, t(66) = 0.39, p = .70, while the gap between the two ratings gave t(66) = 20.67, p < .001, and all 67 scored rights above feminists. In their second experiment 31 women and 40 men stopped in a square in a large Portuguese city, mean age 25.37, rated women's rights at 12.58 and feminist movements at 5.21, F(1, 69) = 429.05, p < .001, η2 = .861, with no difference between male and female respondents. The attempt to close the gap moved less. Telling French women they had forgotten the role of feminists, through a female experimenter, shifted attitudes by 0.54 points where the three more threatening arrangements shifted them by -0.95, -0.77 and -1.45, a contrast of F(1, 54) = 8.35, p < .006, η2 = .134. The Portuguese study repeated the pattern at F(1, 67) = 8.44, p < .005, η2 = .112, with the one improving cell moving 1.44 points.

replication.headline: The approval gap turns up wherever it is measured, most recently at η2 = .861 in Portugal, and every measurement located comes from one line of researchers.
replication.detail: Four samples in three countries have produced the gap: 926 Spanish adolescents in 1989, 93 participants in 2009, 67 French undergraduates and 71 Portuguese passers-by in 2011. Nobody has published a failure to obtain it. Two things qualify that record. The first is authorship. Mugny and Pérez founded the idea, Butera supervised Vernet's doctorate on it, and Vernet is an author on every later study located. No group unconnected to that lineage was found to have run the measurement. The second is what is being repeated. Each study re-obtains a difference between two ratings, which is a descriptive fact about a sample and needs no theory to produce. The causal claim behind the name, that the minority is forgotten and that forgetting is what lets the idea spread, is not what any of these designs test. The nearest thing to a test is the reassociation manipulation, in which an experimenter tells participants they have forgotten who won them their rights. It shifted attitudes by 0.54 points on a 13-point scale in the French sample and 1.44 in the Portuguese one, and only when the person doing the telling belonged to the participant's own group. No preregistration, no multi-site attempt and no meta-analysis was located.

study.cite: Vernet, J.-P., Vala, J., & Butera, F. (2011). Can men promote feminist movements? Outgroup influence sources reduce attitude change toward feminist movements. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 14(5), 723-733.

limits: The measurement is a gap between two ratings taken minutes apart on the same page, from people who have been handed both labels by the experimenter. It does not show that anyone had forgotten anything, because memory was never asked about. Every sample is European and three of the four are young: Spanish teenagers, French undergraduates, and people stopped in a Portuguese square. The 1989 report is the weakest document in the set. It runs to three pages in a professional bulletin, reports means and p-values with no dispersion or effect sizes, and describes a difference at p < .15 as a differentiation between left and right. Its figures were read off a 200 dpi scan of the printed page, character by character, because the file carries no text layer and no French-language optical recognition was available here. The 2009 paper is paywalled; its sample size, design and result are taken from the abstract Hogrefe deposited with Crossref and from the account Vernet, Vala and Butera give of it in 2011, and its own numbers were not obtained. Butera, Levine and Vernet's 2009 chapter and Pérez and Mugny's 1990 chapter were not read. The Spanish version of the 1989 note is listed below and was not read. The search for other work ran across Crossref's bibliographic index, Semantic Scholar's citation graph in both directions from the 2009 paper and the 2009 chapter, Cambridge Core, PubMed and the open web; OpenAlex refused every query with a quota error and was not searched.
misreadings: The first misreading is the name. Cryptomnesia in the memory literature is a person reproducing a word or an idea they heard ten minutes ago and taking it for their own invention, measured item by item in a laboratory that Brown and Murphy built in the same year Mugny and Pérez borrowed the word. The two share a metaphor and no method. Mugny and Pérez's reference list runs to three items, all of them minority-influence work by themselves and by Moscovici, and none of them about memory. Reading across from one literature to the other imports an evidence base that does not apply. The second is the direction of the historical claim. That feminists won women's rights, that anti-racists won racial equality, that these movements were minorities when they started, is argued from history and taken as given by the experiments. What the experiments add is the attitude gap sitting on top of it. The third is the size of what has been shown. Popular accounts describe a society that has forgotten its debts, which is a claim about hundreds of millions of people. The data are four European samples rating five slogans, the largest of them 926 Spanish teenagers. The fourth concerns the remedy. Telling people they have forgotten who won their rights improved attitudes to that group by 0.54 points on a 13-point scale in France and 1.44 in Portugal, and only when the messenger belonged to the same group as the listener. A male experimenter delivering the same reminder to French women left them 0.77 points worse. Last, the 1989 left-right result is sometimes read as showing that the right forgets and the left remembers. Both sides endorsed the principles alike, 7.22 on the left against 7.19 on the right, and the differences that opened when the groups were named ran from 6.25 against 6.03 to 5.70 against 5.33 on an eight-point scale.

sources.text: Mugny, G., & Pérez, J. A. (1989). L'effet de cryptomnésie sociale. Bulletin Suisse des Psychologues, 7, 3-5. The paper that names the effect and the source of every 1989 figure here. Read from the scan on Juan A. Pérez's own publication page at the University of Valencia; the file has no text layer, so the figures were read off the page images.

Vernet, J.-P., Vala, J., & Butera, F. (2011). Can men promote feminist movements? Outgroup influence sources reduce attitude change toward feminist movements. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 14(5), 723-733. Read in full from the University of Lausanne repository; the source for both 2011 experiments and for the account of the 2009 study's design.

Vernet, J.-P., Vala, J., Amâncio, L., & Butera, F. (2009). Conscientization of Social Cryptomnesia Reduces Hostile Sexism and Rejection of Feminists. Social Psychology, 40(3), 130-137. Abstract read as deposited at Crossref and as listed at the Swiss repository sonar.ch; the full text is paywalled and none of its own statistics were obtained.

Vernet, J.-P., & Butera, F. (2005). Women, women's rights and feminist movements. Social Science Information, 44(1), 175-188. The argument that feminist movements are victims of social cryptomnesia, stated without new data. Abstract read at Crossref in English and French.

Butera, F., Levine, J. M., & Vernet, J.-P. (2009). Influence without credit: How successful minorities respond to social cryptomnesia. In F. Butera & J. M. Levine (Eds.), Coping with Minority Status, pp. 311-332. Cambridge University Press. The English-language account the 2011 paper points readers to. Metadata verified at Crossref; the chapter itself was not read.

Moscovici, S., Lage, E., & Naffrechoux, M. (1969). Influence of a Consistent Minority on the Responses of a Majority in a Color Perception Task. Sociometry, 32(4), 365. The study Mugny and Pérez credit with signalling the effect before they named it. Metadata verified at Crossref; the paper was not read.
Mugny, G., & Pérez, J. A. (1991). El efecto de criptomnesia social. Anthropos, 27 suplementos, 110-112. The Spanish version of the 1989 note, listed on Pérez's publication page. Not read.

Brown, A. S., & Murphy, D. R. (1989). Cryptomnesia: Delineating inadvertent plagiarism. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 15(3), 432-442. Cited here only to mark the individual-memory phenomenon that shares the word. Metadata verified at Crossref.
